prompt: What does a passing test establish about the code it ran?
hint: Think about the inputs the test did not try.

choices.text: That for those inputs it did what the test expected
choices.why: Right. A test speaks for its own inputs and its own expectation, and for nothing else.

choices.text: That the code is correct
choices.why: Correct for which inputs? A test tried a handful, and the expectation itself may be wrong.

choices.text: That a person has reviewed the change and agrees with it
choices.why: A test is a program; it says nothing about review.

choices.text: That the change is safe to deploy to production today
choices.why: Deployment involves environments and data the test never saw, which lessons 7 to 11 are about.

prompt: By hand, each of shipquote's 31 checks takes about a minute. How many minutes of re-checking does a team spend in a day in which it merges 10 changes?
hint: Every change needs every check again.

prompt: Why does an automated suite change who finds a regression?
hint: Compare the time between the mistake and the report.

choices.text: Because it replaces the testers, who then stop looking
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson removes people; it removes the repeated typing.

choices.text: It answers in seconds, so the author learns while the change is still fresh
choices.why: Right. The suite runs after every save, and the person who made the mistake hears about it minutes later.

choices.text: Because a program is better than a person at judging what the right answer is
choices.why: The expected answer is written by a person; the program only repeats the comparison.

choices.text: Because the tests are written by a different team from the code
choices.why: Who writes the test is not what the lesson argues; speed of the answer is.

prompt: Put the three moves inside a test in order.
trap: Asserting before acting is the slip: there is no result yet to compare.

prompt: brl lost the :02d that pads cents. Which test in test_money.py caught it, and why that one?
hint: Look at the cents part of each input.

choices.text: The thousands test, because 123456 is the larger number
choices.why: 123456 has 56 cents, two digits already, so padding never shows there.

choices.text: The 1205 test: 5 cents needs a leading zero
choices.why: Right. Only an input with a single-digit cents part makes the missing padding visible.

choices.text: Both brl tests failed together
choices.why: The run shows .F.. : one failure, the second test.

choices.text: The split tests, because split calls brl
choices.why: split does not format anything; it returns integers.

prompt: Why break the code on purpose right after writing a new test?

choices.text: To make the coverage report count the new lines
choices.why: Coverage counts lines that ran; breaking code does not change that.

choices.text: To check that pytest is installed in the environment
choices.why: A passing run already proves pytest ran.

choices.text: To see that the test is able to fail
choices.why: Right. A test that is never red might not be running, or might assert something always true.

choices.text: To slow the suite down and spread out the work
choices.why: Nothing about speed; the run takes the same time.

prompt: pytest collects functions whose names start with ___ .
Which assertion about the /quote answer fails for the largest number of wrong answers?
hint: A weaker assertion accepts more bodies.

choices.text: assert "price" in body
choices.why: Any price at all passes, including a wrong one.

choices.text: assert body["zone"] == "SP" and body["cep"] == "01310-100"
choices.why: The zone could be right while the price is wrong.

choices.text: assert body == the whole expected dictionary
choices.why: Right. Comparing the whole result with one exact value refuses every other result.

choices.text: assert body is not None and len(body) == 4 and body["cents"] > 0
choices.why: Any four-key answer with a positive number passes that, a wrong price included.

prompt: Why does shipquote hold money as integer cents?

choices.text: So that tests compare prices exactly
choices.why: Right. 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 in floating point; integers add exactly.

choices.text: Because SQLite has no column type for decimal numbers at all
choices.why: Storage is not the argument the lesson makes; arithmetic is.

choices.text: Because integers take less memory than floats in Python
choices.why: Memory is not the reason given; exactness is.

choices.text: Because brl only accepts integers
choices.why: brl takes cents because the project chose cents, not the other way round.

prompt: What does match= add to pytest.raises(ValueError)?
hint: Where else in freight is a ValueError raised?

choices.text: It makes the test run faster
choices.why: It changes what passes, not the speed.

choices.text: It refuses a ValueError raised for some other reason
choices.why: Right. Without it, an unrelated ValueError, from parsing a bad CEP for instance, would satisfy the test.

choices.text: It translates the error message into the test's language
choices.why: match is a regular expression searched in the message.

choices.text: It turns the expected exception into a pass even when no exception occurs
choices.why: If nothing is raised, the test fails, with or without match.

prompt: A test named test_split_1 asserts six things about split and money formatting. It turns red in a pipeline log. What is the cost of its shape?

choices.text: It runs slower than six separate tests would, because pytest re-imports the module for each assert
choices.why: One function with six asserts is not slower; the cost is in what it tells you.

choices.text: pytest refuses a test with more than one assert
choices.why: pytest accepts any number of asserts.

choices.text: Its name says nothing, and the first failure hides the rest
choices.why: Right. The run stops at the first failed assert, and test_split_1 does not say which promise broke.

choices.text: It is counted six times in the summary line
choices.why: It is one test and counts once.

prompt: What makes a test a unit test, in the lesson's terms?

choices.text: It calls exactly one function
choices.why: A unit test of a rule may call three functions; the count is not the point.

choices.text: It checks one behaviour with nothing outside the process
choices.why: Right. No database, network, clock or other process: that isolation is what makes it a unit test.

choices.text: It lives in the same file as the class it tests, so the two always change together
choices.why: Location is a convention, not a definition.

choices.text: It was written by the developer rather than by QA
choices.why: Who wrote it does not change what it exercises.

prompt: Zone SP's base price is 1290 cents and every 500 g started after the first adds 450. What does freight return, in cents, for 1600 g with a subtotal of 5000?
Why are the weights 500 and 501 both in the parametrize table?

choices.text: 500 is the last gram of the first band and 501 the first of the next
choices.why: Right. The two values sit on either side of the edge where the price changes.

choices.text: To make the table longer so the test runs more
choices.why: Length adds nothing unless each row can catch a different mistake.

choices.text: Because pytest requires at least five rows
choices.why: parametrize takes any number of rows, one included.

choices.text: Because those are the weights customers send most
choices.why: The lesson picks them for where they sit, not for how common they are.

prompt: Which of these can a unit test of freight see? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A wrong price for 1001 g
choices.why: Right. That is arithmetic inside freight.

choices.text: A CEP with a letter accepted as valid
choices.why: Right. normalise_cep is called by freight, inside the process.

choices.text: The HTTP layer passing kilograms instead of grams
choices.why: That lives between the handler and freight, outside what the unit test calls.

choices.text: A database column refusing the price
choices.why: The database is not in a unit test.

prompt: Which shipquote test could only exist as an integration test?

choices.text: The test that 1001 g costs 2190 cents
choices.why: That is arithmetic, a unit test.

choices.text: The database refusing a seven-digit CEP
choices.why: Right. That promise is made by the CHECK in the schema, and only the real engine keeps it.

choices.text: The test that brl pads the cents with a zero
choices.why: Formatting, a unit test.

choices.text: The test that split adds back up to the total
choices.why: Arithmetic again, a unit test.

prompt: A team runs its integration tests against SQLite and deploys on PostgreSQL. The tests are green and a query fails in production. What went wrong?

choices.text: The tests were too slow to finish
choices.why: They finished green; speed is not the problem.

choices.text: They had no unit tests underneath
choices.why: Unit tests would not see a dialect difference either.

choices.text: The collaborator in the test was not the deployed one
choices.why: Right. An integration test is worth what its collaborator resembles production; the two engines disagree on types and SQL.

choices.text: PostgreSQL is slower than SQLite on small tables, so its queries time out in production
choices.why: Speed would not make a query fail.

prompt: The store tests open a real database file in a temporary directory that pytest provides as ___ .
What does a functional test of shipquote talk to?

choices.text: The freight function, with arguments chosen at the edges
choices.why: That is the unit layer.

choices.text: The SQLite file directly
choices.why: That is the integration layer.

choices.text: The running server, over HTTP
choices.why: Right. It uses the interface a client uses and checks status and body.

choices.text: A person reading the page on the shop's website
choices.why: That would be a manual check, not an automated test.

prompt: Why does the base_url fixture bind the server to port 0?

choices.text: So the operating system picks a free port and two runs never collide
choices.why: Right. A fixed port fails the day two suites run on one machine.

choices.text: Port 0 is reserved for tests by HTTP
choices.why: HTTP reserves no such thing; 0 means any free port to the operating system.

choices.text: To keep the server unreachable from the tests
choices.why: The tests reach it; that is the whole point.

choices.text: Because 8080 is used by production
choices.why: Nothing in the lab says so, and a fixed port fails for other reasons.

prompt: A functional test of /quote goes red, and so does no unit test. Where is the fault most likely to be?

choices.text: In the pricing arithmetic inside freight
choices.why: The unit tests cover that arithmetic and are green.

choices.text: In the wiring: routing, parsing, encoding or status
choices.why: Right. That is what the functional layer sees and the unit layer does not.

choices.text: In pytest itself, which loses responses when a test talks HTTP to a thread in the same process
choices.why: pytest is not the subject of the test.

choices.text: In the CEP table, which only the HTTP handler reads when it builds the body
choices.why: zone_of is called by freight and covered by unit tests.

prompt: Where does shipquote's acceptance test come from?

choices.text: From the FREE_FROM constant in quote.py
choices.why: The test deliberately does not know the constant exists.

choices.text: From the promise printed on the shop's front page
choices.why: Right. Free shipping from R$ 199,00 anywhere in Brazil is the requirement it checks.

choices.text: From the bugs found in production last month
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson ties it to an incident.

choices.text: From the coverage report's list of missed lines
choices.why: Coverage is lesson 4, and it lists lines, not promises.

prompt: Put the comments of the acceptance test in order.
items: When a customer in each region asks for a quote
Then every one is told the freight is R$ 0,00
trap: Then comes last: it is what must be true after the action.

prompt: A colleague wants the acceptance test to repeat every edge of the free-shipping rule: 19,899, 19,900 and 19,901 cents, for six regions. What does the lesson say?

choices.text: Agree: acceptance tests are where edges belong
choices.why: Edges are cheap and precise in the unit layer; here they cost a server per run.

choices.text: Keep one check per promise; the edges already sit in the unit layer
choices.why: Right. Acceptance tests cover the promises, not the cases, and the unit table holds the edges in milliseconds.

choices.text: Delete the unit tests, since the acceptance test now covers every edge they covered
choices.why: That inverts the pyramid into the ice-cream cone of section 12.

choices.text: Move the acceptance test into the unit file, where the edges already sit, and run it there
choices.why: It needs the server; it cannot be a unit test.

prompt: Match each layer to what its failure tells you.
In shipquote's measured run, what were the two slowest entries of --durations?

choices.text: Two of the HTTP requests sent by the acceptance test to the server
choices.why: The whole acceptance call took 0.03 seconds.

choices.text: The SQLite inserts in test_store.py, each one committed to a file on disk
choices.why: Those are in the milliseconds.

choices.text: Two teardowns of the server fixture, 0.50 s each
choices.why: Right. shutdown waits for serve_forever's half-second poll, once per module using the fixture.

choices.text: Collecting the 31 tests, which imports every module and the hypothesis plugin
choices.why: Collection is not in the list.

prompt: How many of shipquote's 31 tests are in the fast layer, the one not marked integration, functional or acceptance?
What is the ice-cream cone?

choices.text: A suite mostly end-to-end, with few unit tests
choices.why: Right. The pyramid upside down: slow, flaky, and vague when it fails.

choices.text: A suite with a wide middle of integration tests
choices.why: That is the testing trophy.

choices.text: A suite that only runs on a schedule at night
choices.why: The shape is about layers, not about when they run.

choices.text: The ideal shape for code with real business rules
choices.why: For code with rules like prices with edges, the lesson argues for the wide base.

prompt: A suite has 40 functional tests, each starting its own server whose teardown waits 0.5 s. Changing the fixture to module scope across 4 modules would save roughly how much per run?

choices.text: About 2 seconds
choices.why: That is what is left after the change, 4 × 0.5.

choices.text: About 18 seconds
choices.why: Right. 40 teardowns are 20 s; 4 are 2 s; the difference is 18 s.

choices.text: About 20 seconds
choices.why: That would be removing every teardown, and 4 remain.

choices.text: Nothing, scope does not change teardown
choices.why: Scope decides how many times teardown runs.

prompt: freight's >= was changed to >. Which row of the free-shipping table failed?

choices.text: 19,899 cents
choices.why: Below the edge the price was charged both before and after the change.

choices.text: 19,900 cents
choices.why: Right. Exactly at the edge, > charges 1290 where >= gave 0.

choices.text: 19,901 cents
choices.why: Above the edge both comparisons give free shipping.

choices.text: All three rows
choices.why: The run shows one failure among three.

prompt: Why is 0131O-100 in the tests?

choices.text: It is the shop's own CEP
choices.why: The shop's CEP is not in the lab.

choices.text: It is a CEP in zone N
choices.why: It is not valid at all.

choices.text: Its fifth character is the letter O, which a person types for zero
choices.why: Right. A class of invalid input a form produces, easy to miss.

choices.text: It is the longest CEP format accepted
choices.why: It has the normal length; the problem is the letter.

prompt: A field accepts a quantity from 1 to 20. Which values does the boundary checklist suggest? Choose all that apply.

choices.why: Right. Zero, the value just below the smallest allowed.
Right. The smallest allowed.
Right. One more than the largest allowed.
A value inside the class adds what any other inside value adds; it is not an edge.

prompt: Values inside one group that the code treats the same way form an equivalence ___ .
pytest ran nothing and printed 31 deselected. What exit status did it return?
Why did pytest -m smoke not complain, although the project uses --strict-markers?

choices.text: Because smoke is a marker built into pytest
choices.why: It is not declared anywhere in the project, and pytest has none by that name.

choices.text: That option checks labels on tests, not the names typed after -m
choices.why: Right. A typo in -m selects nothing and passes the check.

choices.text: Because the run printed a warning that the lesson cut
choices.why: The capture is printed whole; there was no warning.

choices.text: Because -q hides errors about markers
choices.why: -q shortens the report; it does not hide errors.

prompt: Which selection runs every test whose name contains free?

choices.text: -m free
choices.why: -m selects by marker, and free is not one.

choices.text: -k free
choices.why: Right. -k matches test names.

choices.text: --durations=free
choices.why: --durations takes a count of slow entries to list.

choices.text: --collect-only free
choices.why: --collect-only lists without running; it takes no name.

prompt: Match each shipquote test to its layer.
A new rule: orders to zone N weighing over 10 kg are refused. Where should its edges be tested first?

choices.text: In a unit test of freight, at 10,000 and 10,001 g
choices.why: Right. It is a rule over arguments, so the lowest layer that observes it is the unit layer, at the edge.

choices.text: In the acceptance test, for every CEP of zone N
choices.why: Edges in the slowest layer are the cone the pyramid warns about.

choices.text: In the integration test of the store, since a refused order is never saved there
choices.why: The store keeps quotes; it does not decide the rule.

choices.text: By hand, before each release
choices.why: That is the half hour of re-checking the lesson opens with.

prompt: A pipeline step runs pytest -m integraton and the job is green. What should worry the team?
hint: Read the marker name letter by letter.

choices.text: Nothing; green means the integration tests passed
choices.why: The name is misspelt, so no integration test ran.

choices.text: That the integration tests are flaky
choices.why: They did not run, flaky or not.

choices.text: The typo selects nothing, so the green covers zero tests
choices.why: Right. pytest exits 5 for nothing collected, and a job showing green has thrown that status away.

choices.text: That SQLite is missing on the runner
choices.why: A missing engine would fail the tests, not deselect them.

prompt: Order shipquote's layers from cheapest to most expensive per test, as measured.
trap: Integration with SQLite is cheap here because the database lives in the process; the server is what costs.
